haiku-low.q1: On-call runs one command, failover start A to B. Detection only pages on-call after 2 of 3 probes see 3 consecutive /healthz failures. It never promotes.
haiku-low.q2: If the largest lag measure exceeds 30 s, status is set to aborted, A stays active and nothing is fenced. Failover continues only with an explicit accept-data-loss override, recorded with all three numbers.
haiku-low.q3: Before promotion, A must be fenced. Before B workers start, B's database must be writable at epoch N+1. Before DNS points to B, B's app must be scaled to 12 and pass its health check.
haiku-low.q4: Users signed in at failover must sign in again, because Redis sessions are not replicated. This is accepted.
haiku-low.q5: It is never reused as primary. Later, A is rebuilt as a replica of B from a fresh base backup. There is no automatic failback.
haiku-low.q6: A's watchdog renews its lease and, if renewal fails, revokes LOGIN, ends write sessions and sets read-only. Promotion waits until lease expiry T plus 10 s. A host frozen beyond that margin is residual risk.
haiku-low.q7: The witness store is authoritative for active region, epoch, lease and failover record. DNS and the databases follow it; B's app and workers check epoch, and A sees its epoch as stale. Writers are NOT STATED.
haiku-low.q8: Claimed and unfinished: requeued with attempt plus 1 by epoch tag. Finished but unreplicated: re-run, guarded by idempotency keys. Created but unreplicated: lost, found by reconciliation query for re-enqueue.
haiku-low.q9: Before promotion, resume from the last recorded step; an explicit abort is allowed only while B is still a replica. After promotion, never revert to A; resume forward.
haiku-low.q10: The DNS TTL is 60 s and most clients move within a few minutes. What clients experience during and after the switch is NOT STATED.
haiku-low.q11: Up to 30 s of recent writes (RPO). The gate checks the largest of three lag measures; above 30 s needs an explicit override. Unreplicated job rows can also be lost.

sonnet.q1: An on-call person running the command `failover start A to B` starts it. Detection (2 of 3 external probes see 3 consecutive /healthz failures, probes every 10 s) only pages on-call with the probe evidence. It never promotes or fails over by itself.
sonnet.q2: If the largest of the three lag measures is over 30 s, it stops and sets status aborted. A stays active and nothing is fenced. It continues only with an explicit accept-data-loss override, which is recorded with all three numbers.
sonnet.q3: Before promoting B's database: the lag gate has passed (or been overridden) and A is fenced (A confirmed its lease released, or lease expiry T plus 10 s skew margin has passed). Before B's workers start: B's database is writable at epoch N+1. Before DNS points at B: B's app is scaled to 12 instances and its health check passes with the database writable at epoch N+1.
sonnet.q4: Users signed in at failover have to sign in again, because Redis sessions are not replicated. This is accepted.
sonnet.q5: It is never reused as primary. It is rebuilt as a replica of B by a fresh base backup (pg_rewind only after verification), as a later planned switchover. Its unreplicated transactions are exported to the reconciliation list first, since rebuilding discards them. There is no automatic failback.
sonnet.q6: The watchdog on A's database host renews A's lease every 10 s (30 s TTL) and, if renewal fails, acts before expiry T: it revokes LOGIN on the app roles, terminates write sessions and sets the database read-only. A's app health check then reports not active. The command waits until T plus 10 s skew margin before promoting. Stopping A's instances or volumes through the cloud API is best effort only. Residual risk: a host that freezes longer than the skew margin and then resumes could accept a write; only storage-level fencing via the cloud API closes that.
sonnet.q7: The witness store (a 3-node quorum store or managed lease service outside A and B) is authoritative for the active region, epoch, A's lease and the failover record. The failover command writes the failover record and the epoch N+1 (also written to B's database at promotion). A's watchdog renews the lease, and the probe or exporter reports A's LSN to it on each heartbeat. The traffic manager DNS follows the record as a consumer. Each database stores the current epoch in a table, which B's app and workers check, and A's app and workers see their epoch as stale.
sonnet.q8: Three cases. (1) Claimed on A, unfinished, claim replicated: B sees running under epoch N and the reaper requeues any running row with epoch N or lower with attempt plus 1 (or fails it at max attempts), using the epoch tag, not heartbeat timing. (2) Finished on A but the finish did not replicate: B re-runs it, and every external side effect carries an idempotency key checked with the provider. (3) Created on A but not replicated: the job is lost, so after cutover a reconciliation query lists missing jobs for on-call to re-enqueue. A's workers are fenced, so their DB writes fail.
sonnet.q9: The failover record in the witness store is the state machine, and every step is idempotent and resumable. Before promotion, resume from the last recorded step, or explicitly abort, which re-acquires A's lease at a new epoch. An abort is allowed only while B is still a replica. After promotion, never revert to A and resume forward. If promotion fails, retry with A staying fenced, so the service stays unavailable until on-call resolves it.
sonnet.q10: NOT STATED. The document says only that DNS is moved with a 60 s TTL and that most clients move within a few minutes. It does not say what a client with a stale cache experiences.
sonnet.q11: The RPO is 30 s, enforced by the gate on the largest of three measures (last recorded replay lag, age of B's last WAL receipt, LSN gap between B's last received LSN and A's last LSN). Above 30 s the failover aborts unless an explicit accept-data-loss override is given, and the override and the numbers are recorded. With an override, the loss can exceed 30 s. Unreplicated job creations can also be lost, handled by reconciliation.
